name: Mechanical Circulatory Support

question.stem: A 3-day-old term neonate with a prenatal diagnosis of congenital diaphragmatic hernia develops progressive hypoxemic and hypercarbic respiratory failure with evidence of suprasystemic pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular dysfunction despite maximal conventional ventilation, inhaled nitric oxide, and inotropic support. The neonatology and pediatric surgery teams decide to initiate venoarterial (VA) extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) to provide both respiratory and hemodynamic support.
question.prompt: Which of the following describes the correct cannula placement for standard VA ECMO in this patient?

options.text: A single cannula placed in the right atrium provides both drainage and return of oxygenated blood
Venous drainage cannula in the right internal jugular vein advanced into the right atrium; arterial return cannula in the right common carotid artery advanced into the aortic arch
Venous drainage cannula in the right common carotid artery; arterial return cannula in the right internal jugular vein
Venous drainage cannula in the femoral vein advanced into the right atrium; arterial return cannula in the femoral artery
Venous drainage cannula in the umbilical vein; arterial return cannula in the umbilical artery

explanation.text: VA ECMO provides both gas exchange and hemodynamic (cardiac) support by draining deoxygenated venous blood out of the patient, oxygenating and removing CO2 from it via the membrane oxygenator, and then returning it directly into the arterial circulation, effectively bypassing both the lungs and the heart. This is distinct from VV ECMO, which provides only respiratory support and returns oxygenated blood to the venous system, relying on the patient's own heart to circulate it.
In neonates and small infants, the standard cannulation approach for VA ECMO is cervical cannulation:

items: Venous drainage cannula: placed in the right internal jugular vein and advanced so its tip sits in the right atrium, allowing drainage of systemic venous return.

Arterial return cannula: placed in the right common carotid artery and advanced so its tip sits in the aortic arch, allowing oxygenated blood to be returned directly into the systemic arterial circulation.

explanation.text: The right-sided vessels are used because the right internal jugular vein and right common carotid artery are larger and more accessible than their left-sided counterparts in neonates, and because this approach avoids interference with the aortic arch vessels supplying the brain on the more commonly dominant side. This is why VA ECMO carries a well-known risk of right common carotid artery ligation/sacrifice, with downstream neurologic monitoring implications (higher risk of right-sided cerebral hypoperfusion/thromboembolic events), a frequently tested concept in itself.

content.text: VA ECMO requires separate drainage and return cannulas (or a true dual-lumen catheter design used specifically for VV, not VA, support) — a single right atrial cannula cannot simultaneously drain venous blood and independently deliver arterial return to bypass the heart.
This reverses the vessels — the carotid artery cannot be used for venous drainage, and the jugular vein cannot be used for arterial return; this pairing is physiologically backwards.

Femoral vessel cannulation is the preferred approach in larger children and adults, where vessel size allows adequate cannula placement, but femoral vessels in neonates are typically too small to accommodate ECMO cannulas of sufficient size, making cervical (neck) cannulation the standard approach in this age group.

Umbilical vessels are used for umbilical arterial/venous catheters for vascular access/monitoring in neonates, but they are not used for ECMO cannulation due to inadequate size and flow capacity for extracorporeal circuit support.

bottomLine: In neonates on VA ECMO, the standard cannulation is right internal jugular vein (venous drainage, tip in RA) and right common carotid artery (arterial return, tip in aortic arch) — a classic pairing tested alongside its major complication, carotid artery sacrifice.
